solution: The struggle to extend the right to vote (the franchise) to all adults — regardless of property, gender, race, or other characteristics — was essentially a struggle to extend full and equal political citizenship to all members of society, and to make political rights (and thus democratic participation and self-government) truly universal and inclusive. In earlier times, the right to vote and other political rights were typically restricted to a privileged minority — for example, to propertied men — while the majority of people (including the poor, women, and members of racial or other excluded groups) were denied the franchise and thus excluded from full political citizenship and from a say in their own government. The long struggles to extend the franchise — to abolish property qualifications, to grant the vote to women (women's suffrage), to end the exclusion of racial and other groups, and ultimately to establish universal adult franchise (the right of all adult citizens to vote) — were struggles to make political citizenship genuinely full, equal, and universal, and to give all adult members of society an equal political voice and an equal share in democratic self-government. These struggles were a central part of the historical development and democratisation of citizenship, and of the realisation of the ideal of equal and inclusive citizenship for all. The eventual establishment of universal adult franchise — the right of all adult citizens to vote on equal terms — represents a major achievement of this long struggle, and a fundamental element of full, equal, and democratic citizenship. In India, notably, universal adult franchise was granted from the very beginning of the Republic, to all adult citizens regardless of property, education, gender, caste, or religion — a bold and progressive establishment of equal political citizenship for all, at a time when many older democracies had extended the franchise only gradually.

stem: A society in which some groups are formally citizens but are treated as inferior and denied equal rights in practice has been described as having:
options: Full and equal citizenship for all
Unequal or 'second-class' citizenship for the disadvantaged groups
solution: A society in which some groups are formally recognised as citizens but are treated as inferior and denied equal rights, dignity, opportunities, and participation in practice has been described as having unequal or 'second-class' citizenship for those disadvantaged groups. In such a situation, although the members of these groups hold the formal legal status of citizens, they do not enjoy genuinely full and equal citizenship — they are, in effect, treated as inferior or 'second-class' citizens, subjected to discrimination, exclusion, and the denial of the equal rights, dignity, opportunities, and participation that full and equal citizenship is supposed to entail. Historically, many societies have exhibited such unequal or graded citizenship, in which certain groups — such as racial or religious minorities, women, the poor, the lower castes, or the colonised — while nominally members of the society, were denied equal treatment and equal rights, and were relegated to an inferior, 'second-class' status. The existence of such 'second-class' citizenship — of a gap between the formal equal citizenship promised and the unequal treatment actually accorded to some groups — represents a failure to realise the ideal of full and equal citizenship for all, and it has been the target of many of the great struggles for equality, rights, and full and equal citizenship (such as the civil rights movement, the anti-apartheid movement, the women's movement, and the struggles of the oppressed castes and of colonised peoples). These struggles have sought to overcome 'second-class' citizenship and to secure genuinely full and equal citizenship — the actual, equal enjoyment of rights, dignity, opportunities, and participation — for all groups. The concept of 'second-class' or unequal citizenship thus highlights the important distinction between the mere formal status of citizenship and the substantive, equal enjoyment of citizenship rights and dignity, and it underlines that the achievement of genuinely full and equal citizenship for all — and the overcoming of the discrimination and exclusion that relegate some to an inferior status — remains a central and ongoing challenge and endeavour.

stem: The recognition that citizenship rights have been progressively extended over history shows that citizenship is:
options: A dynamic and evolving idea, whose meaning and scope (who is included, and what rights are enjoyed) have expanded over time through struggle
solution: The recognition that citizenship rights have been progressively extended over history — with civil, political, and social rights being granted to more and more members of society, and full and equal citizenship being extended to previously excluded groups (the poor, women, minorities, the oppressed) — shows that citizenship is not a fixed, static, or unchanging status, but a dynamic and evolving idea, whose meaning, scope, and content have expanded and developed over time, largely through struggle. Over the course of modern history, both the range of rights included in citizenship (civil, then political, then social rights) and the range of people included as full and equal citizens have expanded significantly, as a result of long struggles by excluded and disadvantaged groups and the gradual broadening of the understanding of who is entitled to full and equal citizenship and its rights. This history shows that citizenship is an evolving and contested idea, whose boundaries — of inclusion and of rights — have been, and continue to be, reconsidered, contested, and extended over time. It reminds us that the citizenship rights and inclusion we may now take for granted were often won through long and hard struggles, and that the meaning and scope of citizenship can and does change and develop over time. And it suggests that the process of extending and deepening citizenship — of including more people as full and equal citizens, and of securing for all the full range of rights and the genuine, equal enjoyment of citizenship — is an ongoing one, which continues in the present as new groups and issues press their claims to full and equal citizenship and its rights. The dynamic and evolving character of citizenship — its expansion and development over time through struggle — is an important insight, both for understanding the history of citizenship and for recognising that the realisation of full, equal, and inclusive citizenship for all remains an ongoing task and aspiration.

stem: In a democracy, active and informed participation by citizens is important because:
options: Citizens should leave everything to rulers
The quality and health of a democracy depend significantly on the active, informed, and responsible engagement of its citizens in public and political life
solution: In a democracy, active and informed participation by citizens is important because the quality, health, and vitality of a democracy depend significantly on the active, informed, and responsible engagement of its citizens in public and political life. A democracy is, in principle, government by the people, and it depends for its proper functioning not only on good institutions and the protection of rights, but also on citizens who take an active, informed, and responsible interest and part in public affairs — who inform themselves about public issues, participate thoughtfully in the democratic process (for example, by voting wisely, engaging in public debate and discussion, joining associations and movements, and holding their rulers and representatives accountable), respect the rights of fellow citizens, and are concerned with the common good and the well-being of the community. When citizens are passive, uninformed, apathetic, or disengaged — leaving everything to rulers and taking no active part in public life — the quality and health of the democracy suffer: government may become less responsive and accountable, the interests and concerns of ordinary people may be neglected, and the democratic process may be captured by narrow or powerful interests. Active, informed, and responsible citizen participation, by contrast, helps to keep government responsive and accountable, to ensure that the interests and concerns of the people are represented and addressed, to check the abuse of power, and to sustain the vitality and legitimacy of the democratic process. The importance of active and informed citizen participation reflects the understanding that democracy is not merely a set of institutions or a matter of periodic elections, but a way of collective self-government that depends on, and calls for, the active and responsible engagement of its citizens — and that good, active, and informed citizenship is therefore essential to the health and quality of a democracy. This connects to the broader idea of citizenship as involving not only rights but also responsibilities and active participation, and to the importance of cultivating good, active, and responsible citizens for the flourishing of a democratic society.

stem: The Indian Constitution grants equal citizenship to all Indians and additionally provides special safeguards for certain groups, reflecting an effort to:
options: Combine common and equal citizenship for all with the protection of minorities and the upliftment of the disadvantaged, so as to make equal citizenship genuine for all
solution: The Indian Constitution grants equal citizenship and equal fundamental rights to all Indians, and additionally provides certain special safeguards, protections, and provisions for particular groups — such as the protection of the cultural and educational rights of religious and linguistic minorities (Articles 29 and 30), and reservations and special measures for the upliftment of historically disadvantaged groups (the Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and other backward classes). This combination reflects an effort to combine common and equal citizenship and rights for all Indians with the protection of minorities and the upliftment of the disadvantaged, so as to make equal citizenship genuine and substantive for all groups, including minorities and the historically oppressed. The underlying idea is that granting the same formal citizenship and rights to all, while necessary, may not by itself be sufficient to secure genuinely equal citizenship for groups that are minorities or that have suffered historical disadvantage and discrimination — and that special safeguards for minorities (to protect their distinct identities and prevent their being overwhelmed by the majority) and special measures for the disadvantaged (to help them overcome their disadvantages and enjoy genuine equality of opportunity and participation) may be needed to make equal citizenship real and effective for these groups. The Indian constitutional approach thus seeks to combine the ideal of common, equal citizenship for all with the recognition and accommodation of diversity and the addressing of disadvantage — granting equal citizenship and rights to all, while also protecting minorities and uplifting the disadvantaged — in an effort to secure genuinely full, equal, and inclusive citizenship for all groups in a diverse and unequal society. This reflects the broader effort, discussed in the chapter, to combine equal, common citizenship with the accommodation of diversity and the addressing of the special needs and disadvantages of particular groups, so as to make equal citizenship genuine and inclusive for all. It illustrates one important way in which a diverse democratic society has sought to reconcile the ideal of equal, common citizenship with the reality of diversity and disadvantage, and to work towards genuinely full, equal, and inclusive citizenship for all its members.

stem: The ultimate ideal of citizenship, as brought out in the chapter, is:
options: Full, equal, and inclusive citizenship for all members of society — the equal membership, rights, dignity, and participation of all — combined with the acceptance of the shared responsibilities of membership
solution: The ultimate ideal of citizenship, as brought out in the chapter, is that of full, equal, and inclusive citizenship for all members of society — the equal membership, equal rights, equal dignity, and equal participation of all in the shared life and self-government of the political community — combined with the acceptance by all of the shared responsibilities and obligations that membership of the community entails. This ideal holds that all members of society should enjoy full and equal citizenship: that they should all be recognised and treated as equal members of the political community, entitled to the full and equal enjoyment of the rights (civil, political, and social) that citizenship confers, respected in their equal dignity, and able to participate as equals in the social, economic, and political life and self-government of the community — and that no one should be excluded from full and equal citizenship, or denied its rights, dignity, and participation, on arbitrary grounds. At the same time, the ideal of citizenship involves not only the enjoyment of these rights and this equal membership, but also the acceptance and fulfilment by all of the shared responsibilities and obligations of membership — the duties that citizens owe to the community and to one another, and the active and responsible participation in the common life that good citizenship involves. The ideal of full, equal, and inclusive citizenship for all — the equal membership, rights, dignity, and participation of all, combined with the acceptance of shared responsibilities — is central to the vision of a just, democratic, and inclusive society, and it expresses the aspiration that all members of society should belong fully and equally to, and participate fully and equally in, the shared political community, enjoying its rights and dignity and sharing in its responsibilities and self-government. The realisation of this ideal — the securing of genuinely full, equal, and inclusive citizenship for all, and the overcoming of the exclusion, discrimination, and inequality that have often denied it to particular groups — has been, and remains, one of the central aspirations and ongoing endeavours of democratic and inclusive societies, and it is the guiding ideal towards which the theory and practice of citizenship aspire.
